title: Bronchiectasis: Confirm the Structural Disease, Then Reduce Exacerbations
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is chronic abnormal bronchial dilatation with impaired mucus clearance. Confirm it with appropriate chest imaging, identify treatable causes, obtain sputum microbiology when clinically indicated, and build an airway-clearance/exacerbation plan rather than repeatedly treating every cough with empiric antibiotics.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, daily sputum, hemoptysis and coarse crackles should raise suspicion.
Frequent exacerbations, unusual organisms or disease at a young age should trigger evaluation for underlying causes such as immune deficiency, aspiration, ciliary disease or CF.
differentiate: Bronchiectasis can coexist with asthma or COPD but is not simply severe obstructive lung disease.
An acute increase in sputum volume/purulence, dyspnea or systemic symptoms may indicate an exacerbation; stable chronic colonization does not automatically require antibiotics.
assessment: Assess exacerbation frequency, sputum volume/colour, hemoptysis, dyspnea, exercise tolerance, weight/nutrition, aspiration/reflux symptoms, immune history and prior cultures.
Review inhaled therapies and whether the patient has been taught an effective airway-clearance technique.
workup: High-resolution CT is the structural diagnostic test; use spirometry to characterize airflow limitation and sputum culture during relevant exacerbations or when chronic infection changes management.
Use targeted immune, CF/ciliary, aspiration or autoimmune evaluation when phenotype/history suggests it rather than ordering every etiologic test in every patient.
management: Teach individualized airway-clearance therapy and address exercise, vaccination, smoking exposure and comorbid asthma/COPD when present.
Treat exacerbations using prior/current microbiology, severity and local antimicrobial guidance; recurrent exacerbations or chronic difficult organisms warrant respirology input.
Investigate and manage the underlying driver when one is identified rather than treating infection episodes alone.
medicationSafety: Long-term macrolide or inhaled-antibiotic strategies require specialist-style selection and monitoring; review QT, hearing, interaction and resistance risks where relevant.
Do not prescribe chronic inhaled corticosteroids solely for bronchiectasis without another supported indication such as asthma.
redFlags: New focal chest pain with pneumothorax concern
Significant weight loss or recurrent unusual organisms
counselling: Teach how to recognize an exacerbation and when sputum sampling is useful.
Explain that airway clearance is core treatment, not an optional add-on after antibiotics fail.
followUp: Track exacerbation frequency, lung function, microbiology when indicated and treatment burden; refer for specialist management when disease remains frequent, severe or etiologically uncertain.
examTrap: Calling every chronically positive sputum culture an acute infection and repeatedly prescribing antibiotics without checking for a clinical exacerbation.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is airway clearance plus cause-finding plus microbiology-guided exacerbation care.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society non-CF bronchiectasis clinical expertise and guideline resources

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize Right-Heart Risk and Refer Early
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes. Unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart findings should trigger echocardiographic assessment and cause-directed referral; pulmonary-arterial-hypertension drugs should not be started simply because an echo estimates high pulmonary pressure.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort, syncope/presyncope, edema and signs of right-heart strain are important clues.
Risk rises with connective-tissue disease, chronic thromboembolic disease, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease, HIV and selected drug/toxin exposures.
differentiate: Pulmonary hypertension from left-heart disease or chronic lung disease is managed differently from pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Echo estimates probability and right-heart consequences; right-heart catheterization is the definitive hemodynamic classification test when specialty evaluation warrants it.
assessment: Assess functional limitation, syncope, oxygenation, volume status, JVP/right-heart findings, thromboembolic history, connective-tissue features, sleep/lung disease and medication exposures.
Pregnancy or planned pregnancy requires early specialist input because severe pulmonary vascular disease carries major maternal risk.
workup: Use ECG, chest imaging, echocardiography, pulmonary-function testing and cause-directed labs/imaging to characterize likely group and right-heart impact.
Evaluate chronic thromboembolic disease when clinically plausible and refer for expert hemodynamic confirmation before disease-specific therapy.
management: Treat hypoxemia, volume overload and the underlying cause while arranging pulmonary-vascular/cardiology referral.
Disease-specific pulmonary vasodilator therapy is group- and hemodynamic-specific and should follow expert classification rather than an isolated echo pressure estimate.
medicationSafety: Systemic vasodilator or pulmonary vasodilator therapy can worsen hypotension or gas exchange in the wrong physiologic context.
Diuretic therapy can relieve right-sided congestion but excessive preload reduction may worsen low-output symptoms.
counselling: Explain why defining the cause matters before choosing therapy.
Provide clear emergency precautions for syncope, chest pain, severe dyspnea or rapid fluid retention.
followUp: Ensure specialist referral is closed-loop and monitor function, volume status and oxygen needs while the classification workup proceeds.
examTrap: Starting pulmonary arterial hypertension therapy from an elevated echo-estimated pulmonary pressure without determining the cause or confirming the hemodynamic diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a syndrome first; classification determines treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Pulmonary Vascular Disease resources

title: Sarcoidosis: Multisystem Granulomatous Disease, Not Just an Abnormal Chest X-Ray
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of compatible clinical/radiographic disease, supportive pathology when needed, and exclusion of important mimics. Treatment depends on organ threat and functional impairment; not every asymptomatic radiographic finding needs systemic corticosteroids.
recognize: Pulmonary symptoms, bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, skin lesions, uveitis and constitutional symptoms are common patterns.
Cardiac, neurologic, ocular and significant hypercalcemic disease can be disproportionately dangerous even when pulmonary symptoms are mild.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma, occupational exposures and other granulomatous/inflammatory disorders can mimic sarcoidosis.
Serum ACE is neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific to establish the diagnosis alone.
assessment: Assess cough/dyspnea, visual symptoms, palpitations/syncope, neurologic symptoms, skin lesions, constitutional symptoms and exposure/infection risks.
Perform focused cardiopulmonary, skin, eye and neurologic assessment based on symptoms and phenotype.
workup: Use chest imaging and pulmonary-function testing for pulmonary disease; obtain ECG and organ-directed tests when extrapulmonary involvement is plausible.
Biopsy the safest useful site when tissue confirmation is needed and exclude infection/malignancy before committing to immunosuppression.
management: Observe selected stable asymptomatic disease with structured follow-up.

Use corticosteroid or steroid-sparing therapy when clinically significant organ dysfunction, progressive pulmonary disease or organ-threatening involvement warrants treatment, generally with specialty input.
medicationSafety: Before prolonged immunosuppression, address infection screening, vaccination and bone/metabolic risk according to the regimen.
Do not use corticosteroids reflexively before excluding a clinically plausible infection such as TB.
counselling: Explain that sarcoidosis can affect multiple organs and that treatment is driven by risk/function, not the presence of granulomas alone.
followUp: Track symptoms, lung function/imaging and organ-specific involvement; refer urgently for cardiac, neurologic or ocular red flags.
examTrap: Diagnosing sarcoidosis from hilar adenopathy plus a high ACE level without considering TB, lymphoma or other granulomatous disease.
oneLinePearl: Sarcoidosis requires a compatible syndrome and exclusion of mimics; treat threatened organs, not the x-ray alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society interstitial/granulomatous lung disease expertise

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Specialized Multisystem Care Across the Lifespan
bottomLine: Adults with cystic fibrosis need coordinated CF-centre care for airway clearance, chronic infection, nutrition/pancreatic disease, CF-related diabetes, bone disease, fertility/pregnancy and CFTR-modulator management. Primary care complements—not replaces—the specialized CF team.
recognize: Pulmonary exacerbation may present with increased cough/sputum, dyspnea, fatigue, appetite/weight decline or reduced lung function.
Adult CF care is increasingly multisystem because survival has improved and complications such as CF-related diabetes, liver/bone disease and fertility issues matter.
differentiate: A CF exacerbation is not managed like routine uncomplicated bronchitis; prior airway microbiology and the patient's CF plan matter.
CFTR-modulator eligibility and monitoring are genotype/product specific and should follow current Canadian CF guidance and specialty care.
assessment: Review baseline lung function, current respiratory symptoms, prior sputum organisms/resistance, airway-clearance regimen, nutrition/weight, pancreatic enzyme use, glucose/diabetes status and access/adherence barriers.
Assess fertility/pregnancy goals and medication interactions when relevant.
workup: Use sputum microbiology and lung-function assessment according to the CF care plan; evaluate pulmonary exacerbation severity and complications rather than relying on chest x-ray alone.
Screen multisystem complications according to current CF centre standards.
management: Coordinate with the CF clinic for pulmonary exacerbations, chronic suppressive antimicrobial therapy, inhaled therapies and CFTR modulators.
Maintain airway clearance, nutrition support, pancreatic replacement when indicated and complication-specific management.
medicationSafety: CFTR modulators and chronic antimicrobials have important interaction and monitoring requirements; use the current product/CF-centre protocol.
Do not prescribe an empiric antibiotic for a CF exacerbation without considering previous airway microbiology and specialty plan.
redFlags: Suspected distal intestinal obstruction or significant liver complication
counselling: Reinforce airway-clearance and treatment-burden support without blaming adherence.
Discuss transition, reproductive planning and infection-prevention practices with the CF team.
followUp: Ensure CF-centre follow-up and close the loop on exacerbation cultures, lung function, nutrition and multisystem screening.
examTrap: Treating an adult with CF and worsening sputum as ordinary community bronchitis without reviewing prior organisms or involving the CF plan/team.
oneLinePearl: Adult CF is specialized multisystem chronic care; airway microbiology and the CF team guide respiratory treatment.
sourceBasis: Cystic Fibrosis Canada Canadian Guidelines for CF Care
Cystic Fibrosis Canada CFTR modulator guidance

title: Respiratory Infection in Immunocompromise: Broaden the Differential, Shorten the Delay
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients may deteriorate with muted fever or inflammatory findings and have a broader pathogen differential. Severity, immune defect, exposure history and imaging pattern should drive urgent diagnostics and empiric therapy—not reassurance from a normal WBC or mild initial symptoms.
recognize: Risk depends on the immune defect: neutropenia, impaired cellular immunity, B-cell depletion, transplant and corticosteroid/biologic therapy create different infection patterns.
Common respiratory viruses can produce severe disease, while opportunistic fungal, mycobacterial or Pneumocystis infection may need consideration in the right host.
differentiate: Drug pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, malignancy and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage can mimic infection.
A normal chest x-ray early in severe immunocompromised-host infection does not reliably exclude lower-respiratory disease.
assessment: Define the immune defect, treatment timing/dose, neutrophil status, transplant history, prophylaxis, vaccination, travel/exposures and prior resistant organisms.
Assess oxygenation, work of breathing, hemodynamics and subtle deterioration rather than waiting for classic inflammatory signs.
workup: Use prompt chest imaging and respiratory/microbiologic testing matched to severity and immune defect; CT or bronchoscopy may be needed when routine testing is nondiagnostic and risk remains high.
Obtain cultures before antimicrobials when feasible without delaying time-sensitive therapy in an unstable patient.
management: Escalate hypoxemia, hemodynamic instability, severe neutropenia with respiratory symptoms or rapidly progressive disease to acute specialty care.
Choose empiric antimicrobials according to immune defect, severity, prior microbiology and local guidance, then narrow when diagnostic evidence permits.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic function and major drug interactions matter with broad antimicrobials and transplant/immunosuppressive therapy.
Do not stop essential immunosuppression reflexively without coordinating the risk of rejection/disease flare against infection severity.
redFlags: Hemoptysis or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage concern
counselling: Teach early reporting of respiratory symptoms because immune suppression can blunt usual warning signs.
Maintain current vaccination/prevention plans appropriate to the immune condition.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/PCR/antigen studies and imaging; reassess quickly if outpatient management is selected for a carefully defined low-risk situation.
examTrap: Reassuring an immunocompromised patient with dyspnea because they are afebrile and the WBC is normal.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, absence of fever is weak reassurance—define the immune defect and act on physiology.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada respiratory-infection guidance for higher-risk/immunocompromised populations
Canadian infectious-disease and transplant practice principles

title: Thoracentesis: Diagnostic Question, Ultrasound Guidance, Complication Awareness
bottomLine: Thoracentesis should answer a diagnostic or therapeutic question. Confirm a safely accessible pleural collection, use ultrasound guidance where available/standard, send studies matched to the differential, and monitor for pneumothorax, bleeding and re-expansion or respiratory complications.
recognize: New unilateral or otherwise unexplained pleural effusion often requires diagnostic sampling unless the cause is already clinically clear and responding as expected.
Large symptomatic effusions may need therapeutic drainage when the procedure's benefit outweighs risk.
differentiate: Parapneumonic infection/empyema, malignancy, heart failure, hemothorax and chylous effusion have different fluid-testing and management pathways.
Not every bilateral effusion in clinically obvious decompensated heart failure needs immediate diagnostic thoracentesis if it responds as expected and no atypical features exist.
assessment: Assess respiratory status, effusion size/location, bleeding history/antithrombotics, infection/sepsis, prior imaging and whether the result will change management.
Review local scope/credentialing and procedural support before proceeding.
workup: Use bedside/formal ultrasound to identify fluid and a safe site when available; send pleural protein/LDH and additional pH, glucose, cell count, Gram/culture, cytology or specialized tests according to the differential.
Use paired serum studies when required for exudate/transudate interpretation.
management: Perform under appropriate sterile, monitoring and local procedural standards.
Suspected complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema or hemothorax generally needs more than a one-time diagnostic tap and should trigger chest drainage/specialty pathways.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic management is procedure- and patient-specific; use current institutional/specialty guidance rather than a universal hold interval.
Avoid aggressive fluid removal without monitoring symptoms/pressure tolerance in high-risk situations.
counselling: Explain the diagnostic question and the symptoms that require immediate post-procedure reporting.
followUp: Review all pleural-fluid results and imaging; ensure malignancy/infection findings reach definitive follow-up rather than ending with the procedure.
examTrap: Ordering thoracentesis because an effusion exists without asking what the result will change—or sending the same broad pleural panel for every patient.
oneLinePearl: Thoracentesis is a question-driven procedure: safe access, targeted studies, closed-loop results.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory procedural practice
Canadian pleural-disease and ultrasound-guided procedure principles

title: Mechanical Ventilation Basics: Oxygenation, Ventilation, Pressure, and Cause
bottomLine: Ventilator management starts with the patient's physiology: oxygenation, CO2/pH, work of breathing, airway pressure and the cause of respiratory failure. When a ventilated patient suddenly deteriorates, assess the patient and circuit immediately rather than responding to the alarm label alone.
recognize: FiO2/PEEP primarily support oxygenation; minute ventilation changes CO2 clearance.
High airway pressure can reflect obstruction, secretions, bronchospasm, biting, reduced compliance, pneumothorax or circuit problems; low pressure/volume can indicate disconnection or leak.
differentiate: Hypoxemic failure and hypercapnic ventilatory failure require different physiologic adjustments even when both use mechanical support.
Ventilator alarms are clues, not diagnoses; sudden hypotension/hypoxemia after intubation raises tension pneumothorax, auto-PEEP, equipment or tube-position concerns.
assessment: Assess airway/tube position, chest rise, breath sounds, oxygenation, hemodynamics, mental/sedation state and ventilator waveforms/pressures with the critical-care team.
Review the underlying cause, especially obstructive disease, ARDS/pneumonia, pulmonary edema, neuromuscular weakness or metabolic drive.
workup: Use blood gases and imaging when they answer oxygenation/ventilation or complication questions; interpret trends with ventilator settings and patient effort.
When immediate equipment failure is possible, disconnect and manually ventilate with appropriate support while troubleshooting according to acute-care protocol.
management: Use lung-protective ventilation principles where indicated and titrate oxygen to avoid both hypoxemia and unnecessary prolonged hyperoxia.
Correct the underlying process and address dyssynchrony, secretions, bronchospasm, fluid status and sedation/analgesia rather than treating the ventilator number alone.
medicationSafety: Sedation, analgesia and neuromuscular blockade require explicit indications and monitoring; oversedation can prolong ventilation while inadequate analgesia/synchrony can worsen harm.
Non-invasive ventilation and chronic home ventilation have separate evidence-based indications and should not be generalized from invasive ICU ventilation.
counselling: For families, explain the physiologic goal and daily reassessment of support/weaning rather than describing the ventilator as the treatment for the underlying disease.
followUp: Use daily readiness/weaning assessment and complication prevention in acute care; chronic/home ventilation requires dedicated respiratory specialty follow-up.
examTrap: Responding to a high-pressure alarm by simply increasing the pressure limit without checking for obstruction, bronchospasm or pneumothorax.
oneLinePearl: Ventilator alarms point to physiology—assess the patient, airway and circuit before changing numbers.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Home Mechanical Ventilation guidance

title: Asthma-COPD Overlap: Preserve Asthma Safety While Treating Fixed Obstruction
bottomLine: Some adults have persistent airflow obstruction plus convincing asthma features. Do not erase the asthma component: inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy remains important when asthma is present, while COPD bronchodilator, smoking/exposure reduction, vaccination and rehabilitation principles are added according to phenotype and symptoms.
recognize: Asthma features include variable symptoms, atopy/eosinophilic pattern and meaningful reversibility/variability; COPD features include persistent post-bronchodilator obstruction, smoking/occupational exposure and progressive exertional symptoms.
The label is less important than identifying which treatable features and medication-safety rules apply.
differentiate: Persistent obstruction in an older smoker does not prove COPD if the history strongly supports asthma.
Asthma with fixed remodeling and COPD with eosinophilic inflammation can overlap phenotypically; use spirometry/history rather than age alone.
assessment: Confirm inhaler technique/adherence, symptom pattern, exacerbation history, smoking/vaping/occupational exposure, eosinophilic/atopic clues and comorbid rhinitis, GERD, obesity or OSA.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator testing and prior variability evidence where available; do not use a single normal office peak flow to exclude asthma.
Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin testing or alternate diagnoses when COPD appears unusually early or disproportionate.
management: If asthma is part of the phenotype, maintain an inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimen rather than LABA monotherapy.
Add long-acting bronchodilation according to persistent symptoms/exacerbation risk, and address pulmonary rehabilitation/exercise, vaccination and smoking/exposure cessation.
medicationSafety: LABA monotherapy is unsafe in asthma; an asthma component changes the inhaled-therapy floor.
Balance inhaled corticosteroid benefit against pneumonia/thrush and other adverse effects, especially when the COPD phenotype dominates and asthma evidence is weak.
counselling: Use a written action plan and demonstrate inhaler technique.
Explain that overlap means treating both relevant disease mechanisms, not simply adding every available inhaler.
followUp: Track exacerbations, symptoms, inhaler technique/adherence and spirometric trajectory; step therapy according to response and adverse effects.
examTrap: Treating a patient with clear asthma features and fixed obstruction with LABA monotherapy because spirometry also meets COPD criteria.
oneLinePearl: When asthma is truly present in overlap disease, preserve ICS-containing asthma safety while adding COPD-directed care.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current Asthma and COPD guidance
Canadian Thoracic Society asthma/COPD overlap resources
